title: The Target Has More Than One Shape
source: Target Transcription-Factor States, Not Pockets; Drug Discovery Online 2026-08-21
evidence: Author final-audited manuscript and structural/clinical references
review_status: NARRATION AUDITION ONLY; no website deployment

scenes.text: A transcription factor is not a rigid lock waiting for a key. It shifts, binds partners, touches DNA, and changes what a cell can express.
A single protein can populate several conformations. Only some support a particular disease program. The question becomes: which state should a drug change?
An allosteric compound binds away from the functional interface, yet alters how the complex behaves. Binding alone does not prove that regulatory change occurred.
Crystallography offers detailed snapshots. Nuclear magnetic resonance, exchange measurements, and experiments in intact cells can test motion and coupling that static pictures miss.
Consider HIF two alpha. Belzutifan engages a cavity in its P A S B domain, disrupting association with the partner called A R N T.
That mechanism reached patients, but pocket mutations can weaken binding. The resistance problem asks whether the same disease-driving complex can survive by another route.
TEAD proteins show a different opportunity: a central lipid-associated pocket linked to Hippo pathway signaling. Inhibiting this machinery raises questions about isoforms and healthy tissue.
Mutant p fifty-three turns the logic around. The Y two-twenty C substitution destabilizes a tumor suppressor. Rezatapopt aims to stabilize a functional conformation rather than inhibit it.
The evidence must follow the event. First demonstrate engagement, then the predicted state transition, then transcriptional change, and finally a phenotype dependent on that target.
A striking reporter signal is not enough. Target-null controls, resistant alleles, partner measurements, and orthogonal assays can expose a persuasive but misleading mechanism.
Effective concentration matters too. A tight binder in purified protein may never reach sufficient unbound concentration in a living tumor. Exposure connects chemistry with biology.
The opportunity is not that every transcription factor now has a pocket. It is that a regulatory state can become a falsifiable pharmacological target.
